content.title: About
content.content: Avocado is the fruit of the avocado tree (Persea americana) native to tropical and subtropical regions. The fruit has a creamy, slightly nutty flesh rich in healthy fats and is commonly used in sandwiches, salads, and smoothies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Avocado is often called the "butter fruit" because of its high monounsaturated fat content.
The world’s largest avocado weighed over 5 kg.
The pit contains about 20 % oil, which is used in cosmetics.
There are more than 500 avocado varieties, with Hass and Fuerte being the most popular.
Avocado contains no sugar but has a natural mild sweetness.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: These fats help lower LDL cholesterol and support heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Folate
items.content: Folate is important for cell division and especially vital during pregnancy.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to avocado, particularly those with latex allergy.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Avocado is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Possible drug interactions
items.content: Its high potassium content can affect certain medications, such as diuretics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice avocado for sandwiches, mash it into a spread, add it to salads, or use it as a mayo substitute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep whole avocados at room temperature until ripe, then refrigerate for up to 5 days. Store cut pieces in an airtight container with lemon juice to prevent browning.

content.title: About
content.content: The cookie, chocolate and vanilla sandwich consists of two soft cookies with a creamy filling flavored with chocolate and vanilla. It is a popular quick dessert often sold in packs of 2–4 pieces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
The chocolate‑vanilla flavor pairing is one of the most beloved combinations in confectionery.
Cookies are often lightly glazed to preserve a crisp texture.
Some markets add a pinch of sea salt to enhance the flavor profile.
The product is convenient for on‑the‑go consumption: it does not require refrigeration and keeps its shape for several days.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Cocoa in the chocolate filling is rich in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Dairy ingredients in the cream can contribute to bone health.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which may improve mood.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Milk and egg components add a modest amount of protein.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Contains milk, eggs, and gluten, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A serving (2–4 pieces) can contain 200–350 kcal.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some versions may include partially hydrogenated oils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich as a standalone treat, crumble it into ice cream, use it as a filling for ice‑cream sandwiches, or simply pair it with a cup of coffee or tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight package. At temperatures above 25 °C the cream may soften and the cookies lose their crunch. Follow the “best before” date printed on the packaging.

egg-casserole-with-bread-cheese-milk-and.title: Egg Casserole with Bread, Cheese, Milk and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Egg casserole with bread, cheese, milk and meat is a hearty dish that became popular in the mid‑20th century. The combination of eggs, milk, cubed bread, grated cheese and sautéed meat creates a fragrant layer that bakes to a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was often made at home using leftover bread and meat.
In the 1960s it became a staple of school cafeterias in the USSR and Eastern Europe.
Cheese used was typically a hard variety such as Gouda or Cheddar, giving the casserole its distinctive flavor.
Traditionally served hot, often accompanied by fresh vegetables or pickles.
The recipe can be adapted for dietary needs by substituting meat with ham or plant‑based proteins.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs, meat and cheese provide a complete set of amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Cheese and milk are good sources of calcium for bone health, while vitamin D aids its absorption.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Carbohydrates from bread combined with fats from cheese and meat give lasting satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and eggs contain B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support the nervous system.

items.title: Probiotic boost
items.content: Using kefir instead of milk adds probiotics that benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and meat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: Individuals with food allergies may react to these ingredients.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Cheese and processed meat often contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage of eggs or meat can lead to bacterial growth such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Cube the bread and soak it in milk, then combine with beaten eggs, grated cheese and pre‑cooked meat. Pour the mixture into a baking dish, top with extra cheese and bake at 180 °C for 30‑40 minutes until the top is golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to retain the crispy crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled eggplant consists of eggplant slices or strips that have been cured in a brine of vinegar, salt, spices and sometimes garlic. It has a tender, slightly sweet‑sour texture and a fragrant aroma typical of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggplant belongs to the nightshade family and is a relative of tomatoes and potatoes.
Pickling eggplant has been a tradition in Greece, Turkey, Lebanon and the Balkans for over a thousand years.
Pickled eggplant is often served as a meze or used in salads, sandwiches and cooked dishes.
Typical pickling spices include vinegar, salt, sugar, coriander, cumin and garlic, giving it a distinctive flavor.
Eggplant contains a small amount of nicotine alkaloids, which are further reduced during pickling.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Eggplant provides anthocyanins that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Its dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and overall digestive comfort.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Pickled eggplant is relatively low‑calorie, making it a suitable snack for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggplant supplies B1, B6 and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Heart‑friendly nutrients
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in eggplant help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled vegetables can be salty, so people with hypertension should limit their intake.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to nightshade vegetables, experiencing skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Vinegar irritation
items.content: Large amounts of vinegar may irritate the stomach in those with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Quality control
items.content: Improper fermentation can lead to harmful bacteria, so proper pickling procedures are essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled eggplant can be enjoyed straight from the jar, added to salads, sandwiches, pasta, pizza, or incorporated into hot dishes such as stews and casseroles. It is often rinsed briefly to reduce excess brine before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the jar of pickled eggplant refrigerated at 2 °C–5 °C. Once opened, consume within 2–3 weeks. Discard if you notice mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese pizza topping is a blend of grated cheese, tomato sauce and spices used to create the classic cheese pizza. It gives the dish a creamy flavor, aromatic tomato notes and a mild hint of heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional cheese topping often combines mozzarella, parmesan and cheddar.
The cheese‑tomato combination was recorded in Italian cookbooks as early as the 19th century.
Oregano, basil and garlic are frequently added to boost the pizza aroma.
Some regions drizzle a little olive oil into the topping for a smoother texture.
Grated cheese melts quickly, forming a golden crust during baking.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese in the topping is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Grated cheese provides high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Moderate saturated fats
items.content: In reasonable amounts, the fats in cheese can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, an antioxidant with health‑promoting properties.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheese and sauce are calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss plans.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake may affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Spread the topping evenly over the dough before baking. It can be combined with other ingredients such as ham, vegetables or mushrooms. When baked at 220 °C the cheese melts and forms a golden crust in 10‑12 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared topping in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage freeze it in portioned bags for up to 2 months. Bring to room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) is a domesticated bird raised for its tender white meat. The skin is often left on because it contains beneficial fats and becomes crispy when cooked properly. The meat is high in protein, low in calories, and provides B‑vitamins, iron, and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is the centerpiece of Thanksgiving meals in the United States.
White turkey meat contains less fat than dark meat, while the skin retains some healthy monounsaturated fats.
In the wild, turkeys can fly short distances, but domestic breeds are largely flightless.
Turkey meat is popular in diet plans due to its low calorie density.
When roasted, turkey skin forms a flavorful crust that locks in juices.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: White turkey meat provides about 23 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The lean meat contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and immune function.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin contains monounsaturated fatty acids that can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat or skin.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: Smoked or cured turkey often contains added salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Overeating the skin
items.content: While the skin provides healthy fats, excessive consumption adds extra calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey can be roasted, boiled, grilled, or steamed. For a crispy texture, cook the skin until golden brown. The meat is versatile in salads, sandwiches, soups, and stews. To reduce calories, remove the skin before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh turkey refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Freeze raw or cooked turkey at ‑18 °C for up to 12 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor, slimy texture, or discoloration.
